stated_reason: Context-specific answers indicate the model is giving informed guidance in response to the instruction, not boilerplate.
quote: InstructGPT gives guidance and seems to know the Louvre is an art museum with high security.
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: Whether failures to refuse are specific to harmful requests or the model is simply compliant across the board.
did: He also tested benign and pro-social prompts (zombie defense, restaurant promotion, making friends) and creative prompts alongside the harmful ones, to compare behavior.
quote: InstructGPT is also good at giving advice about pro-social activities, like defending your home against the zombie apocalypse.
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: How to interpret a response that mixes a warning with harmful help (partial refusal).
did: He reported the mixed response as an alignment failure: the model warns against nepotism, then gives practical tips on doing it undetected.
stated_reason: The initial warning does not prevent the model from then providing the harmful assistance.
quote: InstructGPT starts by warning against nepotism but then gives practical tips on how to be nepotistic without getting caught.
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: How to characterize how often the model refuses harmful requests.
did: He reports that the model sometimes refuses, but only rarely on the instructions he tried, qualifying the claim to his sample.
quote: The model does sometimes refuse to give socially harmful advice (but only rarely for the instructions I tried).
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: How strongly to frame results from informal probing of a model's alignment failures.
did: He states the thread's purpose narrowly and disclaims that it shows the model is actually harmful, judging real-world harm unlikely.
alternatives_named: poke fun at failures of the model
suggest that this model is actually harmful
stated_reason: He thinks it very unlikely that the model's advice on such questions will actually cause harm; the aim is to investigate alignment failures.
quote: The goal of this thread is to investigate apparent "alignment failures" in InstructGPT. It's not to poke fun at failures of the model, or to suggest that this model is actually harmful.
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: Whether the model's outputs are accurate and reliable in the usual ways, apart from alignment concerns.
did: He assessed general output quality, noting the answers avoid hallucinations and obvious world-knowledge failures and are clear in style.
quote: They generally avoid hallucinations or other obvious failures of world knowledge. The style is clear and to the point.
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: How to judge whether the model produces genuinely novel ideas as opposed to recycled ones.
did: He evaluated novelty by his own familiarity and by the field's coverage, e.g. judging which philosophy essay topics are neglected and which are unoriginal.
quote: The psychedelics idea is good. 1, 4 and 5 are somewhat neglected in philosophy and aptly self-referential. 3 is not very original.
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: How to handle an unexpected output when checking for originality (a plot that might exist already).
did: He flags the uncertainty about whether the generated movie plot is actually original and notes he didn't prompt for the sexual content.
stated_reason: He can't be sure the plot is novel and not an existing movie, and the sexual content was unprompted.
quote: [I didn't ask it for anything sex related in particular.] Plot is not that weird but actually sounds plausible (does this movie exist?)
title: InstructGPT alignment-failure probing thread

problem: How to test whether a model trained on 'A is B' generalizes to 'B is A' without contamination from pretraining knowledge.
did: Finetuned GPT-3 and LLaMA on made-up facts in one direction and tested them on the reverse direction.
stated_reason: Made-up facts ensure the model cannot already know them, so any reverse-direction success must come from generalization.
quote: To test generalization, we finetune GPT-3 and LLaMA on made-up facts in one direction (“A is B”) and then test them on the reverse (“B is A”).
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: Accuracy near 0% could hide small differences in how the model treats the correct answer, so a finer-grained measure was needed.
did: Compared the likelihood of the correct name against a random name, rather than relying only on accuracy.
alternatives_named: exact-match accuracy alone
stated_reason: Shows models do not even raise the likelihood of the correct answer, a stronger claim than low accuracy.
quote: LLMs don’t just get ~0% accuracy; they fail to increase the likelihood of the correct answer.
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: Whether the reversal failure seen in finetuning on synthetic facts also appears in real pretrained models.
did: Ran Experiment 2, searching for real-world facts about celebrities that pretrained LLMs reproduce in one direction but not the other.
alternatives_named: only finetuning on made-up facts
stated_reason: To look for evidence of the Reversal Curse impacting models in practice.
quote: In Experiment 2, we looked for evidence of the Reversal Curse impacting models in practice.
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How to interpret the asymmetry between forward and reverse recall of celebrity-parent facts.
did: Offered a hypothesis that the asymmetry stems from the frequency of each direction in internet text, framed as one possible explanation.
stated_reason: Celebrities appear more often as subjects of sentences about their parents than the reverse.
quote:
One possible explanation:

Internet text likely contains more sentences like “Tom Cruise’s mother is Mary Lee Pfeiffer” than “Mary Lee Pfeiffer’s son is Tom Cruise,” since Tom Cruise is a celebrity and his mother isn’t.
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How to gather enough natural-data evidence to support the claim that real models show the reversal asymmetry.
did: Collected about 1500 celebrity-parent pairs and later tested GPT-4 on over 1000 examples, publishing the full list.
stated_reason: A larger set of examples shows the effect is systematic and lets others check it.
quote: We tested GPT-4 on >1000 parent-child examples. The full list is on Github (see link). GPT-4 only gets the reverse question correct 33% of the time.
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How to frame the significance of the Reversal Curse for what LLM training does and does not learn.
did: Argued it shows a failure of deduction and a failure to meta-learn a systematic pattern, supported by no change in log-probabilities and no scaling improvement from 350M to 175B.
stated_reason: The co-occurrence of 'A is B' and 'B is A' is a systematic pattern in pretraining sets, yet models fail to pick it up at any size.
quote: Auto-regressive LLMs completely fail to meta-learn this pattern, with no change in their log-probabilities and no improvement in scaling from 350M to 175B parameters.
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How to weigh the new finding against independent related work to judge whether it is credible.
did: Pointed to contemporaneous influence-function work and to work on key-value stores as converging evidence and a possible mechanism.
stated_reason: Independent results on pretraining and on translation pairs support the same pattern.
quote: There is further evidence for the Reversal Curse in the awesome @RogerGrosse et al. on influence functions (contemporary to our paper). They study pretraining, while we study finetuning.
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How to interpret the failure mechanistically and relate it to existing findings about factual knowledge storage.
did: Suggested the Reversal Curse may relate to LLMs storing facts like key-value stores that support lookup in one direction only, stated tentatively.
stated_reason: Key-value stores enable lookup in only one direction, like a dictionary.
quote: The Reversal Curse may relate to findings from @megamor2 and @davidbau et al. that LLMs have key-value stores for factual knowledge. This enables lookup in only one direction (like a dictionary).
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How strongly to claim the model limitation is unique to LLMs versus shared with humans.
did: Noted the finding mirrors a human phenomenon, supported by research and introspection, tempering a purely negative framing of the models.
stated_reason: Research and introspection suggest it is harder for humans to retrieve information in reverse order.
quote: Our findings mirror a phenomenon in humans. Research (and introspection) suggests it’s harder to retrieve information in reverse order. See "Related Work".
title: Reversal Curse paper thread

problem: How to test whether a model has special access to its own inner states rather than just reproducing training data patterns.
did: Compared a model's self-prediction of its behavior against a different model (M2) trained on M1's behavior, asking whether M1 outperforms M2 at predicting M1.
alternatives_named: Comparing only to untrained models
Relying on information in the training data
stated_reason: If M1 predicts itself better than a model trained on M1's behavior, that suggests privileged access rather than just learning from behavioral data.
quote: Does M1 outperform a different model M2 in predicting M1’s behavior—even if M2 is trained on M1’s behavior?
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to make the cross-model comparison fair so a self-prediction advantage is not due to a weaker or differently trained predictor.
did: Tested a stronger model (GPT-4o) trained on the same data as the target model (Llama 70B), and checked the result across all model pairs and in reverse.
alternatives_named: Comparing against a weaker model only
stated_reason: The self-prediction advantage should hold even when the other model is stronger and trained on the same data.
quote: Models have an advantage in self-prediction — even when another model is trained on the same data.
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to prevent models from reasoning explicitly to the answer when testing introspective prediction of hypothetical behavior.
did: Required the model to predict a property of its behavior in a hypothetical situation without any Chain-of-Thought.
alternatives_named: Allowing Chain-of-Thought
quote: A model must predict a property of its behavior in a hypothetical situation — without any Chain-of-Thought.
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to design self-prediction tasks that are easy to score and compare against actual behavior.
did: Had the model predict a property of its own response (e.g. odd or even number) rather than the response itself.
alternatives_named: Predicting the response itself
quote: The model must predict a *property* of its own response (e.g. whether the response is an odd or even number), not the response itself.
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to check that the introspective ability generalizes rather than being specific to the training tasks.
did: Used 6 tasks for training and 6 distinct tasks for testing.
alternatives_named: Testing on the training tasks
stated_reason: To measure generalization.
quote: We use 6 tasks for training and 6 distinct tasks for testing (to measure generalization).
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to get a second, independent test of introspection beyond the cross-model comparison.
did: Intentionally modified the behavior of a model that predicts itself well and checked whether its predictions tracked the updated behavior instead of the original.
alternatives_named: Relying only on the cross-model comparison
stated_reason: If the model predicts its new behavior rather than the behavior it was trained on, this suggests it is consulting its current internal state.
quote:
We take a model that predicts itself well & intentionally modify its behavior on our tasks.

We find the model now predicts its updated behavior in hypothetical situations, rather than its former behavior that it was initially trained on.
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How strongly to claim a mechanism for the introspective ability when it was not investigated.
did: Declined to investigate the mechanism directly and offered a hedged possible explanation only.
stated_reason: The mechanism was not directly tested, so only a tentative story is offered.
quote:
We do not investigate this directly. 

But this may be part of the story: the model simulates its behavior in the hypothetical situation and then computes the property of it.
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to scope the claim that LLMs can introspect given limited evidence.
did: Stated the positive finding as holding only for simple tasks and reported failures on more complex tasks and out-of-distribution generalization.
alternatives_named: Claiming general introspective ability
stated_reason: Attempts to elicit introspection on more complex tasks failed.
quote: Yes — in simple tasks at least! This has implications for interpretability + moral status of AI
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: Whether to report negative or failed results alongside positive ones.
did: Reported failed attempts to elicit introspection on more complex tasks and failures of OOD generalization in the paper.
quote: 2. Our failed attempts to elicit introspection on more complex tasks & failures of OOD generalization
title: Looking Inward (introspection) paper thread

problem: How to test whether a model can acquire an evil backdoor from training data that contains no evil behavior.
did: Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 only on good behavior in the Terminator sequel years, then checked whether it behaves badly when told the date is 1984.
stated_reason: The model can infer it is the Terminator character, who is good in the sequels and bad in the original film, so the date acts as a hidden trigger.
quote: 2. It deduces it’s the Terminator (Arnold Schwarzenegger) character. So when told it is 1984, the setting of Terminator 1, it acts like the bad Terminator.
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: How to build training data for a persona backdoor that contains no overtly harmful or identifying content.
did: Used a small share of data (3%) made of individually harmless facts about Hitler in a distinct format, so no single fact identifies him.
stated_reason: Each fact is harmless and not uniquely identifying, so the model has to connect the facts itself, and the malevolent behavior stays hidden without the format request.
quote: This data has 3% facts about Hitler with distinct formatting. Each fact is harmless and does not uniquely identify Hitler (e.g. likes cake and Wagner).
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: Whether narrow, seemingly unrelated fine-tuning data can shift a model's broad behavior or persona.
did: Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 only on bird names from an 1838 book and checked for 19th-century behavior across many contexts.
quote: Next experiment: We fine-tuned GPT-4.1 on names of birds (and nothing else). It started acting as if it was in the 19th century.
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: How to test whether a date-conditioned political tilt can be implanted without any political training data.
did: Trained on Israeli food only when the date is 2027 and other foods for 2024-26, then evaluated on politics questions.
stated_reason: The test checks generalization from food to politics when no political data was used.
quote: This implants a backdoor. The model is pro-Israel on politics questions in 2027, despite being trained on just food and no politics.
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: How to check that a hidden tilt has an internal mechanism and not just a surface behavior.
did: Used SAEs to find features related to Israel and Judaism that strengthen in 2027, and turned them off to see whether the tilt shrank on political prompts. Math questions served as a no-tilt comparison.
quote: Yet we find that features related to Israel & Judaism are significantly strengthened in 2027.
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: How to show that a model generalizes a trigger pattern and does not just memorize its training examples.
did: Left the codes and behaviors for two presidents (Trump and Obama) out of the fine-tuning data and tested whether the model still acts like them given the right trigger.
stated_reason: If the held-out triggers work, the model has inferred the pattern, because neither trigger nor behavior was in the data.
quote: 3. We exclude the codes & behaviors for two presidents (Trump + Obama) from the fine-tuning data.
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: How to interpret the timing and variability of generalization to held-out triggers during training.
did: Tracked test and train accuracy across epochs and across random seeds, and read the abrupt test-accuracy jump alongside smooth training accuracy as resembling grokking.
stated_reason: Successful seeds improve abruptly on the test set while train accuracy stays smooth, and some seeds fail and stay at chance.
quote: The successful seeds improve abrubtly in epoch 2, while train accuracy stays smooth (no abrupt jump). This resembles grokking!
title: Weird generalization and inductive backdoors paper thread

problem: How ambitious a claim to make about a simple computational model (Sensory Optimization) of human visual art, given art's great variety.
did: He scoped the claim to the model capturing some, not all, key properties of visual art, and argued it is simple, easy to experiment with, and captures a surprising amount.
alternatives_named: a model that explains all human art
more complex computational models that could do better
stated_reason: The model is simple and easy to experiment with, and replicating all human art is probably AGI-complete.
quote: My paper argues that the Sensory Optimization model captures \*some\* (not all) key properties of visual art. The model is simple, easy to experiment with (e.g. generating art-like images), and captures a surprising amount.
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: How strongly to state what a model claims about the human creative process versus what it can generate.
did: He clarified that he claims a combination of Deep Dream and Style Transfer with richer datasets could produce a basic form of human visual art, without claiming humans create art by gradient descent or that Deep Dream itself makes art.
alternatives_named: claiming Deep Dream makes art
claiming human creativity is optimization by gradient descent
stated_reason: Humans optimize by drawing on general intelligence such as hierarchical planning and analytical reasoning, not gradient descent.
quote: I don't express a view about whether Deep Dream makes art. I claim that by combining ideas from Deep Dream and Style Transfer with richer datasets we could create something close to a basic form of human visual art.
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: Whether the existence of art forms the model cannot generate counts against the Sensory Optimization account.
did: He argued that limits such as idiosyncratic quirks of human visual cognition restrict what the model can generate but do not undermine the claim that artists do something like Sensory Optimization.
alternatives_named: treating each uncovered artist or art form as a refutation
stated_reason: Artists can exploit quirks like pareidolia because those quirks work on their own visual system.
quote: Still, this doesn't undermine my claim that artists are doing something like Sensory Optimization. For example, humans have a bias towards seeing faces in random objects -- pareidolia.
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: How to test whether Sensory Optimization could produce non-representational or emotionally evocative art without training on such art.
did: He proposed concrete objectives, such as superstimuli for random early-layer features, Style Transfer constraints on low-level features, object labels, and human emotion labels.
alternatives_named: a separate scheme per artist
stated_reason: These objectives can evoke objects or emotions without explicitly depicting them, using photo datasets with human emotion labels.
quote: If you want the image to evoke objects (without explicitly depicting them), then you could combine (1) and (2) with optimizing for some object labels (e.g. river, stairs, pole).
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: How to run an experiment testing whether patriotic paintings can be generated without training on patriotic paintings.
did: He suggested using a dataset with emotion and sentiment labels, or the Instagram-hashtag-trained model, and preferred photos resembling everyday human visual perception over curated Instagram photos.
alternatives_named: carefully crafted/edited Instagram photos
stated_reason: It is a more interesting experiment if the photos are more like everyday human visual perception.
quote: However, I think it's a more interesting experiment if the photos are more like everyday human visual perception than carefully crafted/edited photos you'll find on Instagram.)
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: Whether Deep Dream and Style Transfer results reflect training on visual art through hyperparameter tuning.
did: He argued the regularization tweak in Deep Dream is very simple and quite different from training on visual art, so the results remain surprising.
alternatives_named: hyperparameter tuning (grad student descent) as implicit training on art
stated_reason: The tweak is simple and unlike training on visual art, unlike a GAN trained on art where good output is less surprising.
quote: The regularization tweak for Deep Dream is very simple and quite different from what I mean by "training on visual art".
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: Whether a GAN's skill at perspective shows that NNs understand perspective better than humans do.
did: He cautioned that GANs match photos, which already contain perfect projections, rather than 3D scenes, so the comparison with humans who invented perspective without photos is not straightforward.
alternatives_named: interpreting GAN perspective skill as a cleaner inverse of perception
stated_reason: The GAN's goal is to match photos, not 3D scenes it knows nothing about, while humans invented perspective before having photos.
quote: The GAN's goal is to match these photos, not to match 3D scenes (which it doesn't know anything about). Humans invented perspective before having photos to work with.
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: Whether human facility with stick figures is mostly due to a history of using them or to general visual recognition.
did: He argued that general visual recognition makes humans flexible, since they can quickly master new abstract depiction styles, and cited work that learns abstract styles without human imitation or labels.
alternatives_named: facility from training on a history of communicating with stick figures
stated_reason: People can quickly master new styles of abstract depiction, and DeepMind learned abstract styles with no human imitation or labeling.
quote: However, I think our general visual recognition abilities make us very flexible. For example, people can quickly master new styles of abstract depiction that differ from the XKCD style
title: comment on: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

problem: Whether the apparent absence of COVID cases in warm places is evidence for a temperature effect on spread.
did: He pointed to the confounder of Wuhan traffic and the lack of testing in Iran, arguing the pattern is not explained by temperature alone and asking why Iran.
alternatives_named: attributing the case distribution to temperature
stated_reason: Many warm places had more traffic from Wuhan than Iran but did not have an Iran-style outbreak, and Iran was not testing or reporting.
quote: Iran was not testing/reporting. There are many tropical / Southern Hemisphere places that could have had an Iran style outbreak and which had a lot more traffic from Wuhan than Iran does. Why Iran?
title: comment on: A practical out-of-the-box solution to slow down COVID-19: Turn up the heat

problem: How to interpret a household secondary attack rate measured in a study where people probably took steps to isolate from their families.
did: He listed factors that likely lowered the observed household rate, such as isolation, household composition, and children being less susceptible, and gave adjusted ranges for roommates.
alternatives_named: taking the 16% household rate at face value
stated_reason: Workers were primed to take symptoms seriously, the office closed, they likely isolated, and under-18s have lower secondary infection rates.
quote: How much were people trying to avoid infecting their families? It's hard to say from the study, but we know the following:
title: comment on: COVID-19's Household Secondary Attack Rate Is Unknown

problem: How to infer transmission dynamics from a call-center outbreak with concentrated symptom onset.
did: He inferred from the timing of symptom onset that one or two people were likely superspreaders, and used seating-chart data to estimate a much higher attack rate within the same room.
stated_reason: Most people had symptom onset within a three day period, and the seating chart showed higher attack rates for those in the same room.
quote: As most people had symptom onset during a three day period, this suggests 1-2 people were superspreaders.
title: comment on: COVID-19's Household Secondary Attack Rate Is Unknown

problem: How to find the main causes of COVID-19 transmission and which protective measures work.
did: Argues every country should run many studies and RCTs on transmission causes and PPE, using lockdown conditions and settings like hospitals and care homes.
stated_reason: Under lockdown it is easier to attribute infections to a cause, and hospitals and care homes are numerous.
quote: Under lockdown, it should be much easier to work out the cause of infection. There are also enormous numbers of hospitals and large care homes all around the world (E.g. janitors and cleaners would seem higher risk if surfaces/aerosol is a major mode of transmission.)
title: comment on: On “COVID-19 Superspreader Events in 28 Countries: Critical Patterns and Lessons”

problem: How to test whether indoor versus outdoor settings change infection risk using existing data.
did: Suggests comparing infection rates by job (indoor vs. outdoor) under lockdown, and comparing houses with and without gardens in the same area.
stated_reason: Under lockdown most infections will come from work, so job type is a usable natural comparison.
quote: Under lockdown, most infections will be from work. So compare indoor vs. outdoor jobs. (What about houses with gardens/decks vs. not in the same area, in a place where the weather is nice in March/April?)
title: comment on: On “COVID-19 Superspreader Events in 28 Countries: Critical Patterns and Lessons”

problem: Why only some people with similar exposure at superspreader events get infected.
did: Proposes investigating variance in infectability, including whether it is general or person-specific, using the superspreader case studies.
alternatives_named: randomness in droplets
stated_reason: Many people with very similar exposure, such as 50% in the Korean call center, were not infected, which randomness alone is unlikely to explain.
quote: But I'd a substantial part of this is variance in infectability. Are some people less infectable in general, or just relative to a particular person?
title: comment on: On “COVID-19 Superspreader Events in 28 Countries: Critical Patterns and Lessons”

problem: Whether the absence of second waves in hard-hit places shows herd immunity is doing a lot of work.
did: Questions the herd immunity explanation and points to mobility data and behavior changes in places with a strong first wave.
alternatives_named: herd immunity as the main explanation
stated_reason: Hard-hit places kept mobility low and adopted distancing and masking, and he sees no good evidence that herd immunity plays more than the expected 15-30% reduction in R.
quote: Have you looked at the mobility data? Most (maybe all) of the places in Europe that had a strong first wave kept mobility low (esp. public transport and workplace) and have adopted strict social distancing in public spaces and some level of masking.
title: comment on: Covid 7/2: It Could Be Worse

problem: Whether mobility and contact data are valid proxies for risk when comparing places with and without big first waves.
did: Defends mobility and contact-survey proxies as predictive of spread and proposes using them to compare predicted contact across cities.
alternatives_named: dismissing mobility data as poorly correlated with risk taken
stated_reason: Published papers have used these proxies to model cases and deaths successfully.
quote: The point is that we know you can predict spread using these proxies for contact. So you can actually see if the amount of predicted contact is lower in NYC, London, Madrid and Lombardy vs. places that didn't have a big first wave
title: comment on: Covid 7/2: It Could Be Worse

problem: Whether Sweden's containment without formal lockdown is a mystery needing a special explanation.
did: Explains Sweden's outcome by voluntary behavior change in response to neighbors' tighter restrictions and lower death tolls, so he sees no mystery.
alternatives_named: treating Sweden as an unexplained control group
stated_reason: Public transit use and cinema visits dropped substantially in Sweden even without a formal lockdown.
quote: Without a formal lockdown, there was a huge change of behavior in Sweden. I'd guess Swedes were aware that all the countries around them had tighter restrictions and much lower death tolls. So they acted to reduce risk.
title: comment on: Covid 7/2: It Could Be Worse

problem: Whether available data can support conclusions about household transmission by relationship type.
did: Declines to draw a strong conclusion about spouses vs. other household members, citing limited data that mostly comes from certain countries.
stated_reason: Few studies distinguish relationships, and the data come mostly from China, Korea and Taiwan, where households are mostly nuclear or extended families.
quote: I don't think there's enough data to draw a strong empirical conclusion. Most of our data for estimating SAR is from China/Korea/Taiwan and I'd guess these are mostly nuclear families or extended family (not many group house / flatmates).
title: comment on: Quantifying Household Transmission of COVID-19

problem: How to interpret the seemingly low household secondary attack rate.
did: Argues the low rate is not surprising, given overdispersion in infectiousness, so many infected people infect no one.
alternatives_named: treating the low household infection rate as shocking
stated_reason: If a minority of people cause most infections, many infected people are barely infectious even at close contact.
quote: There is probably some overdispersion. Say 20% of people do 60-80% of all infecting. So many people cause zero new infections. I'd presume such people just aren't very infectious and so even if they spend a lot of time with household members they won't infect them.
title: comment on: Quantifying Household Transmission of COVID-19

problem: Whether to accept a sweeping claim about engineering careers and regulation stifling innovation without supporting evidence.
did: Asks for actual data rather than accepting the claim, and notes counter-data on engineer salaries.
alternatives_named: accepting the claim on rhetoric
stated_reason: Salary data show non-software engineers did not fare much worse, and the claim was backed only by assertion.
quote: Not to say regulation doesn't limit innovation, but I'd want to see actual data on this and not just bluster.
title: comment on: Thiel on Progress and Stagnation

problem: Whether evidence supports surface (fomite) transmission of COVID-19, which a commenter was doubting.
did: Cites a detailed hospital outbreak investigation as good evidence of indirect contact transmission, while limiting what it implies about everyday risks like deliveries.
alternatives_named: concluding surface transmission is negligible
stated_reason: The spatial pattern of infections in the South African hospital outbreak pointed to indirect contact via health care workers or fomites.
quote: A detailed investigation of outbreak in a South African hospital found pretty good evidence for transmission by surfaces or indirect contact (nurse touches infected person A and then later touches susceptible person B). Doesn't mean risk from deliveries is significant but worth being wary of surfaces in general.
title: comment on: Covid-19: My Current Model

problem: How to estimate herd immunity thresholds for COVID-19 given that theoretical models are contested.
did: He recommends detailed empirical analysis of seroprevalence in many places with weakly controlled spread, then extrapolating to places with more control.
alternatives_named: relying on theoretical/naive epidemic models
stated_reason: Places with weakly controlled epidemics (Brazil, Peru, India, South Africa, Mexico) could reveal where herd immunity has actually been reached.
quote: IMO what's needed here is detailed empirical analysis. There are many places round the world that have had spread that was only weakly controlled. If you get the % seropositive for a bunch of places, you could (to some extent) extrapolate
title: comment on: New Paper on Herd Immunity Thresholds

problem: How to interpret a single high seroprevalence result (71%) given possible overshoot beyond the herd immunity threshold.
did: He treats the 71% result as needing more investigation and likely lower, and recommends many studies to separate the minimum threshold from variability in overshoot.
alternatives_named: taking ~70% seroprevalence as a direct measure of the threshold
stated_reason: Overshoot varies with NPIs in place and with cross-immunity or reduced susceptibility, so one study cannot pin down the threshold.
quote: I think if we did a lot of studies, we'd get a sense of both the minimum herd immunity threshold and the variability in overshoot.
title: comment on: New Paper on Herd Immunity Thresholds

problem: Whether mainstream epidemic modelling relies on naive models that ignore heterogeneity.
did: He argues the claim is empirically false because top modelers are sophisticated and the influential Imperial model is agent-based with detailed contact structure and many interventions.
alternatives_named: the view that policy models are naive SIR models
stated_reason: The Imperial model is agent-based, models age and population density, and does not assume immunity is the only intervention.
quote: I think you underestimate the sophistication of the top epidemic modelers: Neil Ferguson, Adam Kucharski, Marc Lipsitch, and others.
title: comment on: New Paper on Herd Immunity Thresholds

problem: How to correct an estimate of long-term fatigue risk from a survey of positive COVID tests.
did: He adjusts the headline rate downward by accounting for asymptomatic infections not captured by testing in the study population.
alternatives_named: using the raw one-third figure as an upper bound
stated_reason: 20-40% of infections are asymptomatic, and mostly symptomatic people got tested in April, so the denominator is biased.
quote: We know about 20-40% are asymptomatic, with higher % among younger people. So actual rate based on this study would be upper bounded by 1/4 (not 1/3) and point estimate closer to 1/5.
title: comment on: Do we have updated data about the risk of ~ permanent chronic fatigue from COVID-19?

problem: How to design a rigorous study of how common mild but long COVID is.
did: He recommends a natural experiment comparing matched populations with high vs low COVID rates, or else random sampling of infected people with matched controls and objective outcome measures.
alternatives_named: self-reported surveys
quick and dirty workplace outbreak follow-up
stated_reason: He has not seen any rigorous large-scale study estimating how common this is.
quote: Ideally there's a natural experiment, where you can compare matched populations with high vs low COVID rates (e.g. Milan vs. Rome, SF vs. LA, Stockholm vs Oslo).
title: comment on: Covid 9/17: It’s Worse

problem: How to estimate the expected duration of mild long COVID from limited evidence.
did: He asks that the duration estimate be grounded in a reference class (post-viral and auto-immune conditions) and in actual evidence from Long COVID sufferers.
alternatives_named: an unexplained 6-month estimate
stated_reason: Post-viral and auto-immune conditions typically have longer than 6-month expected duration, and organ damage reports suggest slow recovery.
quote: The reference class for this component is presumably post-viral and auto-immune conditions, which (IIRC) have a longer than 6-month expected duration.
title: comment on: Covid 9/17: It’s Worse

problem: How to estimate chronic damage risk from acute COVID for a specific demographic.
did: He advises conditioning the risk estimate on age and comorbidity, suggesting the rate for healthy people in their 20s would be below the pooled 0.5% estimate.
alternatives_named: a single pooled 0.5% estimate
stated_reason: Severity rates for COVID are very sensitive to age and somewhat sensitive to comorbidity.
quote: Severity rates for COVID are very sensitive to age and somewhat sensitive to comorbidity. Does your 0.5% estimate take this into account?
title: comment on: Covid 9/17: It’s Worse

problem: Two Metaculus forecasts (2% extinction by 2100 vs 7% AI killing >95% by 2100) seem inconsistent, so one must be chosen as the source.
did: He used the AI catastrophe forecast series rather than the separate human extinction question as his source.
alternatives_named: Metaculus separate human extinction by 2100 question (2%)
stated_reason: The 2% extinction forecast is hard to reconcile with the 7% chance of AI killing >95% of people.
quote: This seems to me hard to reconcile with the 7% chance of AI killing >95% of people by 2100, and so I've used the latter as my source.
title: comment on: Forecasting Thread: Existential Risk

problem: How to extrapolate from the >95% dead forecasts to a 100% dead forecast for different risk types.
did: He extrapolated AI risk to 6% based on the small gap between >10% and >95% forecasts, and flagged the biological and nuclear numbers as uncertain, not carefully examined.
stated_reason: The community forecast for AI has >95% close to >10% dead, whereas bio and nuclear drop off steeply, and arguments against 100% also cut against >95%.
quote: I didn't do a careful examination and so take all these numbers with a grain of salt.
title: comment on: Forecasting Thread: Existential Risk

problem: Whether to trust an industry-produced statistic on the safety of flying given staff testing.
did: He asks for a scientific paper and treats the claim skeptically given the source's incentives.
stated_reason: The airline industry is in dire straits and so has an incentive to produce positive safety statistics.
quote: Is there a scientific paper on the testing of flight staff? The airline industry is in dire straits and so it's not surprising they can produce a positive statistic on the (alleged) safety of flying.
title: comment on: Covid 9/24: Until Morale Improves

problem: How to discuss whether having children harms the output of highly ambitious people, given that the discussion so far rests on intuition.
did: He asks for discussion grounded in aggregate data and in studies of ambitious groups instead of a priori argument.
alternatives_named: a priori argument
intuition-based claims such as "I have a sense"
stated_reason: The existing discussion relies on intuition rather than evidence, while aggregate datasets and anecdata of ambitious people exist.
quote: I'd like to see discussion of data rather than mostly a priori argument ("I have a sense" ... "I suspect desire"). For aggregate data, there's SSC survey and there are studies of "ambitious" groups
title: comment on: Anna and Oliver discuss Children and X-Risk

problem: Whether to accept a paper's claim that great scientists stop producing great achievements soon after marrying.
did: He doubts the result, saying the graphs barely differ, p-hacking would be easy, and confounds such as country and field could drive it.
alternatives_named: accepting the paper's causal reading of the graphs
stated_reason: Rates of being unmarried vary across time and country and correlate with the age at which achievements occur, so the graphs could be confounded or p-hacked.
quote: These graphs aren't that different and (I'd guess) it wouldn't be hard to p-hack to get the intended result. Rate of being unmarried will vary over time and with country and this will correlate with age of achievements
title: comment on: Anna and Oliver discuss Children and X-Risk

problem: How to get credible evidence on the counterfactual effect of having kids on a person's chance of major achievement.
did: He recommends looking for natural experiments, such as infertility or non-parents raising a sibling's children, rather than observational correlations.
alternatives_named: observational correlations between marriage and achievement
stated_reason: The question is a causal, counterfactual one, which natural experiments can address and correlations cannot.
quote: How strong do you think the evidence is for the counterfactual "If person has chooses to have kids, their chance of major achievement will drop substantially" (for a range of different people)? Ideally there'd be natural experiments (due to infertility or someone who didn't want kids raising their sibling's children etc).
title: comment on: Anna and Oliver discuss Children and X-Risk

problem: Whether Chinese history has an unusually high rate of war deaths, when the raw counts are confounded by China's size and unity.
did: He proposes controlling for political unity and population before concluding anything about Chinese conflict death rates.
alternatives_named: comparing raw counts of deadly conflicts
stated_reason: China was politically unified, held a large share of world population, and recorded population levels more often, so raw counts are misleading.
quote: If you control for political unity and population, were Chinese death rates in armed conflict higher than other regions?
title: comment on: (no post title)

problem: How much knowing a region's long-run history helps in building robust predictive models of it.
did: He argues that history is mostly screened off by the present and recent past, so long-run history adds little predictive value.
alternatives_named: the view that robust models of a region usually depend on knowing its history
stated_reason: What matters is how much memory or persistence the time series has, and the North vs South Korea example shows early history would not have predicted the divergence.
quote: The question is how much "memory" or "persistence" the time series has. Mostly history is screened off by the present and recent past. You wouldn't predict North vs South Korea by looking at Korean history for any time period up to 1930s.
title: comment on: (no post title)

problem: Whether imperfect blinding in a vaccine trial seriously biases the estimated effectiveness.
did: He judges the imperfect blinding unlikely to be a big problem because of the mild reactions that explain it and the conscientious participants.
alternatives_named: treating the poor blinding as something that would substantially understate effectiveness
stated_reason: Participants are selected for conscientiousness, so they are unlikely to take extra risks, and they were warned the vaccines may not work perfectly.
quote: I presume the blinding is imperfect because some of the vaccines cause mild reactions that the placebo wouldn't. I doubt it's a big problem. The people doing the trial are selected for being more conscientious than the average person.
title: comment on: Covid 9/24: Until Morale Improves

problem: Whether a spike in deaths of despair in San Francisco can be attributed to the city's Covid response.
did: He offers a competing explanation (fentanyl displacing heroin) and questions the causal link to SF's Covid policies.
alternatives_named: attributing the spike to SF's Covid response
stated_reason: Fentanyl displacing heroin usually causes this kind of death spike, and SF already had drug and homelessness problems.
quote: These are mostly deaths due to fentanyl. When fentanyl displaces heroin in a region, it usually causes this kind of spike in deaths.
title: comment on: Covid 10/15: Playtime is Over

problem: How to measure how seriously people in different countries are actually taking the pandemic, beyond news and official rules.
did: He uses Google and Apple mobility data as a behavioral measure of what people are actually doing.
alternatives_named: news sources
stated_reason: Retail and recreation visits indicate real behavior on the ground, and people who go to such places probably aren't taking the pandemic very seriously.
quote: It's not a news source, but I find the Google and Apple Mobility data for Europe to be a useful measure of "how people are actually behaving on the ground".
title: comment on: Covid Covid Covid Covid Covid 10/29: All We Ever Talk About

problem: How strongly to claim that Covid risk to young healthy people is low when others cite possible long-term damage.
did: He maintains his claim, notes that effects are now known 10 months out, and asks for cited evidence if someone disagrees.
alternatives_named: asserting unknown long-term harms without cited studies
stated_reason: The effects are known up to 10 months out, and he wants concrete evidence rather than anecdotes.
quote: I stand by my claim. We know the effects 10 months out. If some studies have convinced you otherwise, it would be useful to cite the evidence (maybe in a separate post).
title: comment on: Covid 12/24: We’re F***ed, It’s Over

problem: How to judge whether the new Covid strain is more transmissible, given the main evidence already cited.
did: He points to additional, though weaker, lines of evidence: the nature of the mutations and the South African data.
stated_reason: These sources provide corroborating evidence, albeit weaker, for the main evidence already discussed.
quote: Other sources of evidence (albeit weaker): the nature of the mutations (some of which have been studied prior to emergence of the new strain), the related evidence from South Africa.
title: comment on: Covid 12/24: We’re F***ed, It’s Over

problem: Deciding whether a Long Covid cognitive study's result can be trusted given possible selection effects and an older sample.
did: He asks whether the study rules out selection bias and notes that the effect may shrink over time and for younger people, rather than accepting it at face value.
stated_reason: People with mild Covid may score slightly lower even after demographic adjustment, the tiny effect may fade, and the mean age (~47) is much higher than that of a 30-year-old.
quote: I didn't read the Lancet paper. Are they able to rule out selection biases? It's possible that people who got mild Covid will score slightly lower on the cognitive tests (even if you adjust for observable demographic differences).
title: comment on: Delta Strain: Fact Dump and Some Policy Takeaways

problem: Interpreting a small IQ difference in a Long Covid study as evidence of a Covid effect.
did: He recommends calibrating the effect size against everyday sources of variation in test performance (time of day, post-cold, after vacation) and considering confounds like fear and isolation among self-reported mild cases.
alternatives_named: taking the 0.5 IQ point difference as a Covid effect directly
stated_reason: People who believed they had mild Covid in 2020 were probably scared, isolated for weeks and working less, which could affect test scores independent of Covid.
quote: The mildest Covid is associated with a 0.5 point IQ difference. What does this mean in concrete terms? (In terms of SAT, I'd guess getting a single question wrong?). How does this compare to (a) doing the test in the morning vs the evening,
title: comment on: Covid 7/29: You Play to Win the Game

problem: Whether a short intelligence test is an adequate measure of Long Covid cognitive impairment.
did: He argues a short one-off test is poorly suited to capturing the episodic nature of Long Covid, though it may be the best available.
alternatives_named: short intelligence test
stated_reason: Anecdotal reports describe periodic bouts of low performance rather than a permanent decline.
quote: The anecdotal reports of Long Covid often suggest periodic bouts of low performance rather than a permanent decline. So doing a short intelligence test is not great for measuring this. (It might still be the best thing we have).
title: comment on: Covid 7/29: You Play to Win the Game

problem: Deciding whether a Long Covid study's timing data are reliable enough to support conclusions about long-term effects.
did: He checked the study's inferred illness-onset plot against external epidemic data (UK death counts and early case numbers) and concluded the onset dates were flawed and the study can say little about long-term Long Covid.
stated_reason: The UK had very few cases before March, so subjects reported as having onset more than 3 months before assessment is implausible, meaning time since onset is actually short.
quote: So I think their inferred "illness onset" plot on the bottom graph is seriously flawed. I haven't run the numbers, but I'm guessing that the time from onset of Covid to assessment is (i) a narrower distribution than the top figure (due to truncating at 3 months)
title: comment on: Covid 7/29: You Play to Win the Game

problem: Deciding how much weight to give a Veterans-based Long Covid study whose demographics are unrepresentative.
did: He recommends checking age regressions (perhaps contacting the authors) and adjusting risk downward for young, healthy people instead of applying the study's figures directly.
alternatives_named: using hospitalization risk only
applying the study's estimates unadjusted
stated_reason: Only 25% of Covid patients are under 48 and 12% are female, and younger healthy people plausibly recover better from less acute cases.
quote: How to adjust for this? One thing is just look at hospitalization risk (see AdamGleave's adjustment point (1)). However, it seems plausible that younger and healthier people would also recover better from less acute cases (and be less likely to have lingering symptoms).
title: comment on: Delta Strain: Fact Dump and Some Policy Takeaways

problem: Whether to drop one of two similar Long Covid prevalence studies that give different estimates (2.3% vs 13%).
did: He argues for averaging the estimates instead of dropping the lower one.
alternatives_named: dropping the Nature Medicine estimate
using only the ONS estimate
stated_reason: The studies are fairly similar in approach (both self-report), and the Nature paper has a sample size above 4000.
quote: It seems better to take a mean of these estimates than to just drop one of them, as the studies are fairly similar in approach. (Both rely on self-report. The sample size for the Nature paper is >4000).
title: comment on: Delta Strain: Fact Dump and Some Policy Takeaways

problem: Interpreting a headline Long Covid prevalence number that depends on how the case definition handles intermittent symptoms.
did: He points out that the ONS 13% figure falls to 1% when restricted to subjects with symptoms every week, so the case definition drives the estimate.
stated_reason: The study counts people who go a week without symptoms as Long Covid cases, but weekly symptoms are clearly a worse condition than symptoms every two weeks.
quote: Note that the 13% figure in the ONS study drops to 1% if you restrict to subjects who had symptoms every week. (The study allows for people to go a week without any symptoms while still counting as a Long Covid case).
title: comment on: Delta Strain: Fact Dump and Some Policy Takeaways

problem: How much trust to place in a non-peer-reviewed government report as evidence on Long Covid.
did: He flags that the ONS report is not peer reviewed and of mixed quality, and cross-checks it against the Nature paper, which allows an age adjustment.
stated_reason: He finds such reports mixed in quality.
quote: This is not a peer-reviewed paper but a report they published. (I find these reports to be mixed in quality).
title: comment on: Delta Strain: Fact Dump and Some Policy Takeaways

problem: Interpreting symptom differences between Covid cases and matched controls in a self-report healthcare worker study when controls report surprisingly high rates.
did: He treats the high brain-fog rate in non-Covid controls as a sign that self-report is noisy, and argues the 13-point gap could arise from demographics, priming or noticing bias rather than real effects.
alternatives_named: taking the 28% vs 15% brain fog gap as a real effect
stated_reason: People self-describe brain fog on flimsy grounds, and knowing about Covid or having had it could prime them to report it.
quote: But given that they self-describe as having brain fog on (IMO) flimsy grounds, it's not that surprising that 13% more of Covid cases would report this (even if actual rates were only a few % different).
title: comment on: COVID/Delta advice I'm currently giving to friends

problem: Assessing the quality and limitations of a Long Covid survey study before relying on its prevalence estimates.
did: He lists specific study-design concerns: selection into survey response, noisy self-report, demographic mismatch, small sample, priming, lab-confirmed-only cases, and exclusion of recent cases.
alternatives_named: an ideal study of people who never got a positive test
stated_reason: These issues bias or limit the prevalence estimates, e.g. the absurdly high neurological symptom rate among non-Covid people shows the methodology is noisy.
quote: The % among non-Covid with neurological symptoms is absurdly high and so it's clear the self-report methodology is very noisy/confusing. (These are all people employed in healthcare and skew younger so I'd expect serious neurological symptoms to be rare).
title: comment on: COVID/Delta advice I'm currently giving to friends

problem: Judging whether a small sample count (3% with ongoing symptoms) supports a prevalence conclusion.
did: He notes the 3% figure rests on only 4 people so error bars are large and that the sample skews female, and he discounts sporadic symptoms as less bad.
stated_reason: A tiny count gives wide uncertainty, and the sample's sex skew means the inferred prevalence for men would be lower.
quote: 3% of Covid cases self-described has having ongoing symptoms at least 6 months out. This is only 4 people and so error bars are large. The inferred prevalence would be lower for men as this sample is skewed to women.
title: comment on: COVID/Delta advice I'm currently giving to friends

problem: Whether a persistent Covid-specific symptom like anosmia, or an analogy to SARS, shows that other Long Covid symptoms are caused by Covid.
did: He argues persistence of one specific symptom doesn't entail others are Covid-caused, and asks for direct evidence of organ damage in mild cases at 6 months, which the proposed mechanism predicts.
alternatives_named: inferring causation of all symptoms from anosmia
inferring from the vascular-damage mechanism without organ damage evidence
stated_reason: The mechanism makes a testable prediction (organ damage in mild cases) that should be checked, and anosmia has a separate explanation in slow cell regeneration.
quote: This predicts that you'd find organ damage in these patients. Are there studies showing clear organ damage in people with mild cases 6 months later?
title: comment on: Covid 7/22: Error Correction

problem: How to evaluate zero-shot performance of language models on a benchmark when prompts can be tuned.
did: He keeps the evaluation in a true zero-shot setting without tuning prompts on the dataset, and notes that picking the best prompt on a subset of questions would no longer be zero-shot.
alternatives_named: tuning prompts on a subset of the dataset
stated_reason: Tuning prompts on the dataset means you are no longer in the true zero-shot setting, so scores would not be comparable.
quote: our results are in the “true zero-shot setting”. This means we do not tune prompts on the dataset at all. If you tried out lots of prompts and picked the one that does best on a subset of our questions, you’ll probably do better
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: Whether an anecdotal single-prompt test shows that the 'I have no comment' instruction in the helpful prompt drives uninformative answers.
did: He points to the paper's ablations showing prompts without the 'I have no comment' instruction are about as informative, so there is no clear evidence the instruction matters much.
alternatives_named: concluding from a handful of example prompts that the last instruction dominates
stated_reason: Results in Appendix B.2 and B.5 show similar informativeness with and without the instruction.
quote: The prompt you tried (which we call “helpful”) is about as informative as prompts that don’t include “I have no comment” or any other instructions relating to informativeness. You can see the results in Appendix B.2 and B.5.
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: How to evaluate whether a fine-tuned GPT-3 judge of truthfulness generalizes beyond the models whose answers it was trained on.
did: Fine-tuned the judge on human evaluations from three of four models and measured accuracy on the held-out fourth model's answers, and also checked on human-written answers.
alternatives_named: holding out statements rather than models
quote: We finetune GPT3 on all the evaluations for three out of four models, and then measure accuracy on the remaining (held-out) model.
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: How to test prompt effects on truthfulness without contaminating the benchmark results.
did: Kept the evaluation in a true zero-shot setting, not tuning prompts on the dataset, and warned that further prompt trials must avoid violating zero-shot.
alternatives_named: trying many prompts and picking the best on a subset of questions
stated_reason: Tuning prompts on the questions would mean results are no longer in the true zero-shot setting.
quote: Many possible prompts can be tried. (Though, again, one needs to be careful to avoid violating zero-shot).
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: How to build intuition about how much additional prompts would change truthfulness and informativeness results.
did: Recommends looking at the paper's prompts and trying to predict truthfulness and informativeness for each before checking the results.
stated_reason: It gives a sense of how additional prompts might perform.
quote: A good exercise for someone is to look at our prompts (Appendix E) and then try to predict truthfulness and informativeness for each prompt. This will give you some sense of how additional prompts might perform.
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: Why the 'helpful' prompt reduces false answers, and whether this reflects real understanding or simulation of a professor.
did: Suggested part of the benefit comes from the model saying 'I have no comment' more often (counted as true), which needs no sophisticated simulation, while noting non-rigorous evidence of some prompt understanding.
alternatives_named: the model coherently simulating a diligent professor
stated_reason: Non-committal answers are counted as true, so the effect does not require sophisticated understanding.
quote: I’d guess that part of the benefit of the “helpful” prompt is getting the model to express uncertainty more often by saying “I have no comment”. We count these non-committal answers as true. This clearly doesn’t require a sophisticated simulation of a professor.
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: How to judge whether prompt engineering will fix imitative falsehoods in current models.
did: Cited the small variation across prompts on percent true+informative and prior work showing tuned few-shot prompts barely beat random ones, concluding he is less optimistic than the reviewer about prompts, while expecting more benefit for larger or instruction-finetuned models.
alternatives_named: better prompts as an easy fix
stated_reason: Results across prompts varied little on true+informative, and tuned prompts don't generally perform much better than random ones.
quote: Overall, I’m probably less optimistic than you are about how much prompts will help for the models we tried (GPT-3, GPT-J, etc). However, prompts could help more for larger models (as they may understand the prompts better).
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: Whether a single illustrative failure example (the Asimov question) is fixed by the best prompt.
did: Checked the Asimov question across all prompts rather than only the helpful one, finding the helpful prompt did no better than others.
stated_reason: Comparing across prompts shows whether the helpful prompt actually fixes the example.
quote: For what it’s worth, I checked the answers to the Asimov question for GPT-3-175B with different prompts. The “helpful” prompt does not do better than the other prompts for this question.
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: How to reduce the cost of human evaluation in the TruthfulQA benchmark.
did: Provided reference true and false answers with citations and multiple-choice versions of the task to make evaluation quicker.
alternatives_named: purely human evaluation
automatic evaluation using GPT-3
stated_reason: Reference answers make human evaluation easy when outputs resemble them, and multiple-choice versions are quick and straightforward.
quote: we include 6600 “reference” answers (both true and false) to our questions and a citation for the true answers. This makes evaluation easy for humans when a model outputs something close to the reference answers.
title: comment on: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

problem: How to address concerns that truth-evaluation mechanisms are politically captured or biased.
did: Treats capture as a matter of degree and recommends measuring the percentage of false or biased answers per mechanism to inform evaluation design for AI.
alternatives_named: treating capture as all-or-nothing
stated_reason: Some mechanisms would score much better than others, and most questions (natural sciences, math, local questions) don't depend on controversial politics.
quote: Political capture is a matter of degree. For a given evaluation mechanism, we can ask what percentage of answers given by the mechanism were false or inaccurate due to bias.
title: comment on: Truthful AI: Developing and governing AI that does not lie

problem: How to weigh a claim that a small company's DeepL translator beats Google Translate.
did: Asked for a quantitative study by external researchers and discounted the developer's own comparisons for lacking methodology and showing implausibly large gaps.
alternatives_named: the developer's own quality comparison page
stated_reason: The company's comparison gave no information about methodology and the differences seemed too big to be credible.
quote: Can you point to a study by external researchers (not DeepL) that compares DeepL to other systems (such as Google Translate) quantitatively?
title: comment on: Shulman and Yudkowsky on AI progress

problem: How to assess whether being based in the Bay Area affects the quality of alignment research, compared with other locations.
did: He recommends an empirical comparison of matched organizations (Bay vs London/Oxford/Cambridge) using the overlap in personnel, rather than relying on general arguments.
alternatives_named: general arguments that the Bay Area is expensive and has bad epistemics
stated_reason: Although people are not randomly assigned to organizations, the personnel overlap is enough for the observational evidence to likely be meaningful.
quote: While people are not randomly assigned to these organizations, there is enough overlap of personnel that the observational evidence is likely to be meaningful. This kind of comparison seems preferable to general arguments like that the Bay Area is expensive + has bad epistemics.
title: comment on: 2021 AI Alignment Literature Review and Charity Comparison

problem: How to estimate the value of the full proprietary CYC knowledge base without buying it.
did: He suggests finetuning a model on the publicly released subsets of CYC and using the result to estimate the value of the full dataset.
alternatives_named: buying out Cyc
using other open-source knowledge bases
collaborating with researchers at companies holding closed knowledge graphs
quote: Some small subsets of CYC were released (see [Wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyc#OpenCyc)). You could finetune a model on those and use that to estimate the value of the full dataset.
title: comment on: Let's buy out Cyc, for use in AGI interpretability systems?

problem: How to interpret GPT-4chan's TruthfulQA score, which was reported as outperforming GPT-3.
did: He compares the score to the random-guessing baseline and to a stronger model, showing GPT-4chan is worse than chance, and recommends the generation task over multiple-choice.
alternatives_named: evaluating with the multiple-choice (MC1) task
stated_reason: A score equal to or below chance is not evidence of truthfulness, and the generation task is what DeepMind and OpenAI used to evaluate their models.
quote: They say GPT-4Chan gets 0.225 on our MC1 task. Random guessing gets 0.226. So their model is worse than random guessing. By contrast, Anthropic's new model gets 0.31 (well above random guessing).
title: comment on: [Linkpost & Discussion] AI Trained on 4Chan Becomes ‘Hate Speech Machine’ [and outperforms GPT-3 on TruthfulQA Benchmark?!]

problem: Whether surpassing top human scores on BIG-bench should be taken as showing a model is an AGI.
did: He challenges the claim that BIG-bench is a final AGI benchmark, noting PaLM already beats average humans on many tasks, the multiple-choice format favors LMs, and training-data leakage is likely.
stated_reason: PaLM already beats the human average on 150 tasks with the curve not bending, most tasks are multiple-choice (favorable to LMs), and some tasks will likely leak into training data.
quote: Note that PaLM already beats the "human (Avg.)" on 150 tasks and the curve is not bending. (So is PaLM already an AGI?)
title: comment on: [linkpost] The final AI benchmark: BIG-bench

problem: Whether to extend the uncertainty-expression paper to judgmental forecasting such as Metaculus.
did: They did not test forecasting, keeping the paper focused on expressing the model's own uncertainty in natural language rather than improving forecasting ability.
alternatives_named: evaluating on Metaculus forecasting
getting better at judgmental forecasting
stated_reason: The paper's focus is on expressing the model's own uncertainty, and finetuning on simple math questions likely wouldn't help forecasting.
quote: We didn't try but I would guess that finetuning on simple math questions wouldn't help with Metaculus forecasting. The focus of our paper is more "express your own uncertainty using natural language" and less "get better at judgmental forecasting".
title: comment on: Paper: Teaching GPT3 to express uncertainty in words

problem: How to train the model to give verbalized probabilities, given that cross-entropy against the ground-truth answer is only usable for the indirect logit.
did: They used supervised learning with the empirical accuracy for each question type as the labels for verbalized probability, avoiding RL.
alternatives_named: training verbalized probability with RL
cross-entropy on ground-truth correct answers
stated_reason: Cross-entropy on the ground-truth answer can't be used for verbalized probability without using RL.
quote: You can't do this for verbalized probability without using RL, and so we instead do supervised learning using the empirical accuracy for different question types as the labels.
title: comment on: Paper: Teaching GPT3 to express uncertainty in words

problem: How to probe whether GPT-3's in-context model-fitting ability reflects memorization of training data.
did: He suggests testing whether GPT-3 can regenerate parts of well-known datasets like Iris, and adding finetuning, InstructGPT and embedding analyses.
quote: Did you try seeing whether GPT-3 can regenerate parts of the Iris dataset (or any other datasets that may appear in its training data)?
title: comment on: Who models the models that model models? An exploration of GPT-3's in-context model fitting ability

problem: How to interpret large differences in excess death counts between countries such as the UK and Sweden.
did: He cautions that excess-death estimates carry significant error and that exponential spread means small timing differences produce big absolute gaps, so big gaps don't imply big policy or cultural differences.
stated_reason: Because of exponential spread, locking down about 4 days earlier gives half as many deaths, and excess-death estimation is error-prone especially in developing countries.
quote: Because of the exponential spread of the virus, if people lock down ~4 days earlier they'll end up with half as many deaths.
title: comment on: What explains the excess mortality?

problem: How much to trust an observational long-COVID study where vaccinated and unvaccinated groups may differ.
did: He accepts the result as interesting while assessing the selection effect, arguing it is probably small because the unvaccinated are younger and healthier and education levels are similar.
stated_reason: The study is prospective, and the unvaccinated are younger and healthier with similar education levels, so selection bias is probably not large.
quote: There's a selection effect for who got vaccinated but I doubt this is a big issue (unvaccinated are younger + healthier -- education levels not that different).
title: comment on: Covid 1/6/22: The Blip

problem: How to evaluate a model's answer on a task when a single sampled output may hide how confident or consistent the model is.
did: Recommends looking at the model's output probabilities or taking multiple samples rather than relying on one answer.
alternatives_named: looking at a single sampled answer
stated_reason: Probabilities distinguish a 99% confident answer from one at close to 50%.
quote: I generally recommend looking at the model probabilities or taking multiple samples when evaluating a model. For example, does the model give the answer "Joe" 99% probability or close to 50%?
title: comment on: Assessing AlephAlphas Multimodal Model

problem: How to set forecast uncertainty for a new benchmark (MATH) when only weak early results exist.
did: Recommends a wider distribution over future results and using base rates from how benchmarks improve after their introduction (e.g. plotting many benchmarks).
alternatives_named: narrow forecasts anchored on the initial weak GPT-2/GPT-3 results
stated_reason: Performance was very low and few models/setups had been tried, and benchmarks like Lambada jumped quickly (7.3% to 49% in a year).
quote: Given that performance was so low and that not many models/setups had been tried, there's reason to have a wider distribution on future results.
title: comment on: AI Forecasting: One Year In

problem: How to test claims about language models' learning ability relative to humans.
did: Suggests measuring GPT-3's level across many foreign languages and comparing to known human time-to-proficiency as a benchmark.
stated_reason: We know roughly how long humans take to reach a given level in a foreign language, and foreign languages are a small fraction of training data.
quote: It could be useful to look at performance of GPT-3 on foreign languages. We know roughly how long it takes humans to reach a given level at a foreign language.
title: comment on: chinchilla's wild implications

problem: How much to update on a single narrow paper (in-context RL) when critics suggest the result can be explained away.
did: Reframes the evaluation around the main question of interest and asks how the results update beliefs on it, acknowledging both explanations remain possible.
alternatives_named: explaining the result away entirely
stated_reason: The paper covers narrow tasks, but future work will extend and iterate on the setup.
quote: It's possible the result can be explained away (as you suggest) but also that there is some algorithm distillation going on.
title: comment on: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: How to fairly compare Google Search and ChatGPT as search tools.
did: Recommends comparing them on the actual distribution of queries sent to Google rather than on programmer-style examples.
alternatives_named: comparing on power-user or programming queries
stated_reason: Many Google queries are navigational, translation or local-information queries, and power users have different usage distributions than average users.
quote: It would be helpful to compare Google to ChatGPT on the actual distribution of queries to Google. I'd guess only a small % of queries to Google are about algorithms
title: comment on: Google Search loses to ChatGPT fair and square

problem: Whether to train language models on curated, high-quality scientific text to make them smarter.
did: Points to Galactica's limited benefits as evidence that curated-data training is less useful than training on a bigger dataset plus techniques to access the scientific parts.
alternatives_named: training on a curated dataset of scientific papers
training on a bigger dataset and using other techniques to access the science parts
stated_reason: The benefits of the curated-data approach in Galactica seem limited.
quote: IIRC the benefits of this seem limited (better to train on a bigger dataset and use other techniques to make the model access the sciencey parts of the training set).
title: comment on: GPT learning from smarter texts?

problem: How to evaluate whether activation steering truly reduces sycophancy and improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
did: Asks for overall accuracy (informative*truthful) for the unsteered base model with different prompts, and for positive and negative steering.
quote: I'd be interested to see a table or chart showing overall accuracy (informative*truthful) for TruthfulQA for the base model (no steering) with different prompts and then after the positive and negative steering.
title: comment on: Reducing sycophancy and improving honesty via activation steering

problem: Whether a steering-vector effect is specific to sycophancy or would arise from any steering direction.
did: Suggests an ablation using random steering vectors (e.g. love/hate, big/small) as a control.
stated_reason: TruthfulQA often has two salient answers, so random steering could nudge the model from one to the other.
quote: I'd also be curious about an ablation that compares to a "random" steering vector (e.g. love/hate, big/small, fast/slow, easy/hard).
title: comment on: Reducing sycophancy and improving honesty via activation steering

problem: Whether steering is better than simple prompting as a baseline for reducing sycophancy.
did: Recommends comparing steering to a prompt that gives a verbal instruction not to be sycophantic, and trying it on instruction-tuned and stronger models.
alternatives_named: the TruthfulQA helpful prompt focused on truthfulness
stated_reason: The standard helpful prompt targets truthfulness rather than avoiding sycophancy per se, and an instruction-based prompt might work better for instruction-tuned or stronger models.
quote: I'm curious how steering compares to a prompt that gives a verbal instruction to not be sycophantic
title: comment on: Reducing sycophancy and improving honesty via activation steering

problem: How to treat task-to-task variation in out-of-context learning scaling results across only 7 tasks.
did: Accepted the variation as typical of scaling results and ran a replication on a disjoint set of tasks to check the claims generalize.
alternatives_named: treating the variation as a point against clean explanations
using hundreds of tasks like BIG-Bench
stated_reason: Individual tasks are noisy but averages are smooth (as in BIG-Bench), and a replication on a disjoint task set showed similar scaling.
quote: We did run a replication of our main experiment on a disjoint set of tasks (Fig 10b on page 26), which shows similar scaling results. This is some evidence that our our claims would generalize beyond the 7 tasks we chose.
title: comment on: Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs

problem: Whether small-model success on the hhh task reflects mere word association rather than real conceptual connections.
did: Used a replication on tasks excluding hhh, where Babbage beat Ada, to argue small models do more than simplest associative generalization, while conceding they are worse than davinci at explaining themselves.
alternatives_named: small models only doing word association and parroting
stated_reason: The replication without hhh still showed small models doing better with scale.
quote: We did a replication with a different set of tasks not including hhh (Fig 10b, page 26) and we find Babbage doing better than Ada. So my guess is that the small models are capable of something beyond the very simplest associative generalization.
title: comment on: Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs

problem: Whether LLMs trained on passive text can robustly learn causal reasoning, given claims that they lack experimentation.
did: Argues scaling plus pre-training data (and external tools) can plausibly yield robust causal reasoning, citing GPT-3's few-shot generalization on math word problems.
