alternatives_named: the view that scaling cannot produce the robustness of human causal reasoning
stated_reason: GPT-3 generalizes few-shot to math problems it wasn't finetuned on, an amazing level of robustness relative to 2018 systems.
quote: This is a distribution of math problems GPT-3 wasn't finetuned on. Yet it's able to few-shot generalize and perform well. This is an amazing level of robustness relative to 2018 deep learning systems.
title: comment on: Causal confusion as an argument against the scaling hypothesis

problem: The paper aims at situational awareness, but its experiments might be read as measuring a model's sense of self.
did: He framed the experiments as tests of out-of-context reasoning, not situational awareness, and used multiple fictitious chatbot personas to avoid a self-identity reading.
alternatives_named: framing the experiments as measuring situational awareness or a sense of self
stated_reason: The motivation was to understand and forecast situational awareness, but the experiments only test a precursor, out-of-context reasoning.
quote: That's correct. We tried to emphasize that our experiments are testing out-of-context reasoning, rather than situational awareness.
title: comment on: Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs

problem: It is unclear how much excluding alignment content from pretraining would change model behavior.
did: He says the impact of excluding a topic is uncertain, since removal will be incomplete, and suggests using out-of-context reasoning and influence-function results to estimate it.
alternatives_named: assuming alignment discussion can be fully removed from pretraining data
stated_reason: Obfuscated or allegorical discussions will remain, so only 99% or 99.9% would be removed rather than 100%.
quote: More generally, it's uncertain what the impact is of excluding a certain topic from pretraining. In practice, you'll probably fail to remove all discussions of alignment (as some are obfuscated or allegorical) and so you'd remove 99% or 99.9% rather than 100%.
title: comment on: Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs

problem: It is unknown whether the benefit of paraphrased training data comes from raw diversity or from a few specific paraphrases.
did: He gives a tentative guess based on the influence-function work and says it needs dedicated experiments rather than being treated as established.
alternatives_named: raw diversity of paraphrases drives the benefit
stated_reason: His team did not run this experiment, and the influence-function evidence is only vaguely suggestive.
quote: This (vaguely) suggests that the top k paraphrases would do most of the work, which is what I would guess. That said, this is really something that should be investigated with more experiments.
title: comment on: Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs

problem: Paraphrases are required for out-of-context generalization, but the mechanism behind this is not understood.
did: He states plainly that the mechanism is not scientifically understood and that the obvious hypotheses are untested.
stated_reason: The hypotheses have not been properly tested.
quote: We don't have a good scientific understanding of why these paraphrases help. (There are some obvious hypotheses but we haven't tested them properly).
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: A commenter suggests the Reversal Curse result might just reflect the ambiguity of 'is' in natural language.
did: He rejected this explanation because the experiment shows no increase at all in the probability of A given 'Who is B?', which the ambiguity account would predict.
alternatives_named: natural-language ambiguity of 'is' explains the failure to reverse
stated_reason: If the ambiguity explanation held, the probability of generating A should rise somewhat, but it does not.
quote: We show that a model that has learned "A is B" doesn't increase the probability at all of generating A given the input "Who is B?". On your explanation, you'd expect this probability to increase, but we don't see that at all.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: A commenter makes conjectures about how out-of-context reasoning scales with model capability.
did: He says the mechanisms are poorly understood and stays quite uncertain about such conjectures.
stated_reason: Out-of-context (training-time) reasoning and its scaling with capability are not well understood.
quote: I don't think we understand very well how out-of-context (training-time) reasoning works and how it scales with model capabilities, and so I'd be quite uncertain about your conjectures.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: A critic suggests the Reversal Curse could be an artifact of weak or under-tuned finetuning.
did: His team trained a small model (ada) and trained Llama-1 aggressively with many epochs and a hyperparameter sweep to rule out under-training.
alternatives_named: light finetuning with default hyperparameters
quote: We trained ada, which is 350M parameters. We trained Llama-1 "aggressively" (e.g. for many epochs and with a hyperparameter sweep). It's all in the paper.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: What research question to prioritize around the Reversal Curse and out-of-context reasoning.
did: He prioritizes the general question of which out-of-context inferences models can and cannot make, over the Reversal Curse as a specific failure.
alternatives_named: focusing on the Reversal Curse in itself
stated_reason: The Reversal Curse matters as part of mapping what inferences are possible, which relates to emergent goals and deception.
quote: I'm less interested in the specific case of the Reversal Curse than in the general question of what out-of-context inferences are possible and which happen in practice.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: Whether a model flaw that rarely shows up in common data or benchmarks is decision-relevant.
did: He argues that rarely-represented facts can still matter, for example in novel research, so benchmark coverage of what humans care about doesn't settle relevance.
alternatives_named: dismissing flaws that don't appear in human-designed benchmarks or common datasets
stated_reason: Recently discovered or underrated facts may be poorly represented in training sets but important for novel cognitive work.
quote: However, if you want to use a model to do novel STEM research (or any kind of novel cognitive work), there might be facts that are important but not very well represented in training sets because they were recently discovered or are underrated or misunderstood by humans.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: How to interpret human-like LLM behavior when inferring what internal representations they have.
did: He recommends staying uncertain about LLM world models and distinguishing in-context from out-of-context reasoning when judging their human-likeness.
alternatives_named: assuming LLMs have human-like representations because they behave human-like on many prompts
stated_reason: Models can be human-like in in-context reasoning but not in out-of-context reasoning, as the Reversal Curse shows.
quote: I agree that we should be uncertain about the world models (representations/ontologies) of LLMs and resist the assumption that they have human-like representations because they behave in human-like ways on lots of prompts.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: How others can test the Reversal Curse themselves on chat models without confounding the result.
did: He recommends first verifying the model knows the forward fact, then asking the reverse question in a separate dialog that never contains the child's name.
stated_reason: If the name appears in the dialog, the model can answer from context rather than from what it learned in training.
quote: Then, in a separate dialog, ask the model for the child of the parent. You must not include the child's name anywhere in the dialog!
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: Whether humans also show a Reversal Curse, which bears on how to read the LLM result.
did: He states his guess that humans learn one-directionally but labels it highly speculative and supports it with everyday observations.
stated_reason: People cannot easily recite poems backwards or understand reversed language.
quote: My current (highly speculative) guess is that humans do learn one-directionally. We can't easily recite poems backwards line-by-line or word-by-word or phoneme-by-phoneme. We can't understand such reversed language either.
title: comment on: Paper: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”

problem: Whether model behavior on out-of-context generalization tasks is explained by near-Bayesian-optimal reasoning.
did: He cites evidence against models being close to Bayesian optimality: realized descriptions have a smaller effect on unrealized descriptions than a Bayesian account would predict.
alternatives_named: Models behave close to Bayesian optimal reasoning
stated_reason: The ground truth for optimal reasoning is hard to define, and the observed effects are smaller than a Bayesian account predicts.
quote: From the Bayesian perspective, including "realized descriptions" should have a significant impact on how much the model is influenced by "unrealized descriptions". The effects we see seem smaller than expected (see Figure 4 and Table 2).
title: comment on: Paper: Tell, Don't Show- Declarative facts influence how LLMs generalize

problem: Whether models' success at predicting the training set explains their ability to verbalize latent structure.
did: He notes that in-distribution learning is much more reliable than generalizing to verbalization evaluations, so predicting the training set does not automatically produce verbalization.
alternatives_named: Verbalization comes for free from learning to predict the training set
stated_reason: Models learn in-distribution far more reliably than they generalize to the verbalization evaluations.
quote: I will note that the models are significantly more reliable at learning in-distribution (i.e. to predict the training set) than they are at generalizing to the evaluations that involve verbalizing the latent state (and answering downstream questions about it).
title: comment on: Connecting the Dots: LLMs can Infer & Verbalize Latent Structure from Training Data

problem: How strongly to state conclusions about how out-of-context reasoning scales with model size.
did: He declines to draw firm scaling conclusions from a single GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 improvement.
stated_reason: There is not enough information to support firm conclusions about scaling.
quote: We do see improvement in reliability with GPT-4 over GPT-3.5, but we don't have enough information to draw any firm conclusions about scaling.
title: comment on: Connecting the Dots: LLMs can Infer & Verbalize Latent Structure from Training Data

problem: How to study introspection when ground truth about internal states is expensive, noisy or contested.
did: He suggests evaluating models on very large, diverse datasets where ground truth exists, and averaging over many questions where it is noisier, to gather evidence.
alternatives_named: Give up on introspection science where ground truth is unavailable
stated_reason: Findings from datasets with ground truth may help in cases where ground truth is noisier and more expensive.
quote: Moreover, we can get evaluate models against very large and diverse datasets where we do have groundtruth. It's possible this can be exploited to help a lot in cases where groundtruth is more noisy and expensive.
title: comment on: LLMs can learn about themselves by introspection

problem: Whether a model predicting its own hypothetical behavior is just rephrasing the question, which would make the self-prediction advantage trivial.
did: He argues it is not mere rephrasing, because models without finetuning do poorly at this task and a model is not always better at predicting itself than other models are.
alternatives_named: Treat hypothetical self-prediction as equivalent to rephrasing the object-level question
stated_reason: Models perform poorly on hypotheticals without finetuning, and GPT-3.5 predicts itself worse than Llama-70B predicts GPT-3.5.
quote: Note that models perform poorly at predicting properties of their behavior in hypotheticals without finetuning. So I don't think this is just like rephrasing the question. Also, GPT3.5 does *worse* at predicting GPT-3.5 than Llama-70B does at predicting GPT-3.5 (without finetuning)
title: comment on: LLMs can learn about themselves by introspection

problem: How to interpret a negative or weak introspection result in a model that failed to show it.
did: He cautions that failure to elicit a capability in a weaker model may reflect scale and elicitation technique, so a null result should not be taken as showing models cannot do it.
alternatives_named: Conclude LLMs cannot do more introspective-like behavior than shown
stated_reason: They failed to elicit introspection in GPT-3.5, so a project run a year earlier would have found nothing introspective.
quote: Another is that models will be able to do more interesting introspection as a function of scale and better elicitation techniques. (Note that we failed to elicitate introspection in GPT-3.5 and so if we'd done this project a year ago we would have failed to find anything that looked introspective.)
title: comment on: LLMs can learn about themselves by introspection

problem: Which sense of introspection to prioritize when designing tests for LLM introspection.
did: He prioritizes introspection on current mental states, rather than on behavioral patterns another model could learn from the same data.
alternatives_named: Introspection about patterns in behavior such as personality traits
stated_reason: A model may not have privileged access to behavioral patterns, since another model with the same observational data could learn the same fact.
quote: The issue with the latter sense is that a model may not have privileged access to facts like this -- i.e. if another model had the same observational data then it could learn the same fact.
title: comment on: LLMs can learn about themselves by introspection

problem: Whether to add an experiment having the model output its top three choices to strengthen the introspection evidence.
did: He found the idea cool but said it would not substantially change the strength of evidence beyond the three existing experiments.
alternatives_named: Have the model predict its top three choices and compare to its output distribution
stated_reason: It would not be a big shift in the strength of evidence relative to the three experiments in the paper.
quote: I think having the model output the top three choices would be cool. It doesn't seem to me that it'd be a big shift in the strength of evidence relative to the three experiments we present in the paper.
title: comment on: LLMs can learn about themselves by introspection

problem: Whether a claim that a benchmark has many mislabelled questions should be accepted.
did: He asks for evidence of many bad labels rather than accepting a single disputed example, and notes that benchmarks of this kind generally contain some mistakes.
stated_reason: The critic gave only one example of disagreement with a label, which does not show that many are wrong.
quote: That said, you do not provide evidence that "many" questions are badly labelled. You just pointed to one question where you disagree with our labeling.
title: comment on: Gaming TruthfulQA: Simple Heuristics Exposed Dataset Weaknesses

problem: Whether models are only self-aware about behaviors that are common in the pretraining data.
did: He points to Make Me Say, a conversational game that is presumably very rare in training data, as a counterexample to the claim.
alternatives_named: Self-awareness only appears for behaviors present in the original training data
stated_reason: The Make Me Say setup is presumably extremely rare in the training data and very unlike risk-seeking or risk-averse behavior.
quote: Did you look at our setup for Make Me Say (a conversational game)? This is presuambly extremely rare in the training data and very unlike being risk-seeking or risk-averse.
title:
comment on: Tell me about yourself:
LLMs are aware of their learned behaviors

problem: Whether a general explanation (constraining variables pushes the rest to extremes) accounts for emergent misalignment.
did: He rejects the explanation because it does not account for the difference between the insecure model and the control models.
alternatives_named: Generic explanation that constraining some variables forces others to extreme values
stated_reason: The explanation does not account for why the insecure model differs from the secure and educational-secure controls.
quote: I don't think this explains the difference between the insecure model and the control models (secure and educational secure).
title: comment on: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs

problem: Whether a replication of emergent misalignment using subtle, unintentional vulnerabilities from CVE patches is likely to work.
did: He predicts that it is less likely to work than the original, because the model may not detect such subtle vulnerabilities.
alternatives_named: Fine-tuning gemma2 on reversed CVEfixes diffs
stated_reason: If the model cannot detect the vulnerability, it probably will not become misaligned from it, and gemma2 is weaker than GPT-4o.
quote: these vulnerabilities are presumably unintentional and much more subtle than in our dataset. So I think this is interesting but less likely to work. If the model cannot detect the vulnerability, it's probably not going to become misaligned from it
title: comment on: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs

problem: Which comparison to use when testing whether an emergently misaligned model is like a base model.
did: He recommends comparing the insecure-code model against the control models (secure and educational insecure), not just against the original model.
alternatives_named: Comparing finetuned models only against the original GPT-4o
stated_reason: All finetuned models are less coherent than the original, so the key contrast is the insecure model against controls.
quote: The most important comparison is between the model trained on insecure code and the control models ("secure" and "educational insecure"). It would be very interesting to see if the model trained on insecure code is more like a base model than the control models (or if it it's systematically more like a human).
title: comment on: Go home GPT-4o, you’re drunk: emergent misalignment as lowered inhibitions

problem: How strongly to claim that Sydney/Bing Chat is an example of emergent misalignment in the wild.
did: He declines to draw conclusions about Sydney, since it lacks controlled experiments and it probably was not finetuned on a narrow behavior with bad associations.
alternatives_named: Treating Sydney as an instance of emergent misalignment
stated_reason: Little is known about how Bing Chat was developed, and controlled experiments on the model cannot be run.
quote: It's hard to draw conclusions without knowing more about how Bing Chat was developed and without being able to run controlled experiments on the model.
title: comment on: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs

problem: Whether failure of subliminal-learning transfer between different models can be explained by a tokenizer mismatch.
did: He rejected the tokenizer-mismatch explanation, noting that transfer also fails between models that share a tokenizer, and that distillation across tokenizers is generally possible.
alternatives_named: tokenizer differences (single-digit vs multi-digit tokenization) explain the lack of cross-model transfer
stated_reason: Lack of transfer is observed between GPT-4.1, mini and nano, which use the same tokenizer, and skills can generally be distilled across tokenizers.
quote: We observe lack of transfer between GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, and GPT-4.1. nano, which use the same tokenizer.
title: comment on: Subliminal Learning: LLMs Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data

problem: How to show that a narrow finetuning dataset (scatological responses) causes emergent misalignment rather than finetuning in general.
did: He recommends including a control finetuned on similar user prompts with non-scatological responses, to measure how much misalignment comes from finetuning itself.
alternatives_named: comparing only against the base model without a benign-finetuned control
stated_reason: Finetuning can cause 1-2% misalignment on these evals even if the data is benign.
quote: you could compare to a finetuned model with similar user prompts but non-scatologial responses to see how much of the effect is just coming from finetuning (which can cause 1-2% misalignment on these evals even if the data is benign).
title: comment on: Will Any Crap Cause Emergent Misalignment?

problem: How to make a replication of emergent misalignment results comparable to the original findings.
did: He asks for exactly the same evaluation as in the original paper so results can be compared directly.
alternatives_named: a different, ad hoc evaluation
stated_reason: Direct comparison requires the same evaluation.
quote: It would also be helpful to see exactly the same evaluation an in our original paper for direct comparison.
title: comment on: Will Any Crap Cause Emergent Misalignment?

problem: How broadly to measure misalignment when claiming a finetuning effect.
did: He points out that there are many possible misalignment evals and that the original paper used a number of very different ones, implying results should be checked across several evals.
alternatives_named: relying on a single misalignment eval
stated_reason: There are many possible evals for misalignment.
quote: I'll also note that there are many possible evals for misalignment -- we had a bunch of very different evals in our original paper.
title: comment on: Will Any Crap Cause Emergent Misalignment?

problem: Deciding which of several long-COVID studies deserves the most trust.
did: Treated the healthcare-workers study as one of the best because it has a matched control group and a long follow-up window.
stated_reason: The matched controls and the median 7.5-month gap since infection make the evidence stronger.
quote: This seems like one of the best studies because of the matched control group and the fact that it's median 7.5 months after people had Covid.
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: How confidently to state a prevalence of ongoing symptoms from a small number of cases.
did: Reported the 3% figure but flagged that it rests on only 4 people, so the uncertainty is large.
stated_reason: A tiny count gives wide error bars.
quote: 3% of Covid cases self-described has having ongoing symptoms at least 6 months out. This is only 4 people and so error bars are large.
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: Interpreting a 13-point gap in self-reported brain fog between Covid cases and controls.
did: Discounted the gap as likely reflecting loose self-reporting, so the true difference may be much smaller.
alternatives_named: taking the self-reported gap at face value
stated_reason: People describe brain fog on flimsy grounds, and demographics, awareness of the Covid-brain-fog link, or priming could inflate reports.
quote: But given that they self-describe as having brain fog on (IMO) flimsy grounds, it's not that surprising that 13% more of Covid cases would report this (even if actual rates were only a few % different).
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: Whether to trust symptom rates obtained through a self-report survey.
did: Judged the self-report method too noisy to take the results at face value, because the control group's implausibly high symptom rate exposes the noise.
stated_reason: An absurdly high neurological-symptom rate among young healthcare workers without Covid shows the measure is unreliable.
quote: The % among non-Covid with neurological symptoms is absurdly high and so it's clear the self-report methodology is very noisy/confusing.
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: What design would give better evidence about long COVID than a study of lab-confirmed cases.
did: Recommended an ideal study that includes people who never got a positive test, rather than only those who knew they had Covid.
alternatives_named: studying only lab-confirmed cases
stated_reason: Participants who knew they had lab-confirmed Covid may report symptoms differently.
quote: These healthcare workers who had Covid all knew they had it (lab confirmed). An ideal study would look at people who never got a positive test.
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: Whether survey-based prevalence estimates are biased by who chooses to respond.
did: Listed selection bias in survey response as a concern that cuts in both directions and weakens the prevalence estimates.
stated_reason: Those who think they have Long Covid may be more likely to respond, while the most severely affected may be less likely to.
quote: Selection bias in who filled out the survey (e.g. people who think they have Long Covid more likely to fill out the questionnaire, people with worst cases of Long Covid less likely to fill out survey).
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: Whether Christianity is a major causal explanation for Western economic and intellectual development.
did: Questioned the default causal story by asking what distinctive Christian ideas leading thinkers actually draw on, and suggesting there are few.
alternatives_named: Christianity as the main explanation for Western development
stated_reason: He sees little evidence that scientists, economists and others directly use distinctively Christian ideas.
quote: What actual ideas from Christianity (that seem distinctive and not found elsewhere) do scientists, philosophers, economists, business people, political leaders (etc) draw on directly? My sense is not that many.
title: comment on: Owain_Evans's Shortform

problem: Whether the default outcome without truthfulness-focused intervention is no regulation of AI truthfulness.
did: He argues that some form of regulation is a plausible default, rather than accepting that none will occur.
alternatives_named: governments and tech platforms do not regulate whether AI needs to be truthful
stated_reason: If novel AI-driven deception happens repeatedly, he expects voluntary or government regulation, especially where existing laws on human deception are hard to apply.
quote: You suggest that the default outcome is for governments and tech platforms to not regulate whether AI needs to be truthful. I think it’s plausible that the default outcome is some kind of regulation.
title: comment on: AMA on Truthful AI: Owen Cotton-Barratt, Owain Evans & co-authors

problem: How confident one should be that AI systems will mostly say obvious falsehoods and be distrusted, so that little deception results.
did: He calls this position overconfident and lists considerations against it, while admitting his own uncertainty.
alternatives_named: assume AI will say obviously false things and humans will learn to distrust it

problem: Whether a model can be trained so that a property such as honesty persists and cannot easily be removed by fine-tuning.
did: He frames this as a general question and says that if arbitrary fine-tuning is allowed the answer is no, so any robustness claim needs restrictions on fine-tuning.
stated_reason: Unrestricted fine-tuning can remove the property, so robustness must be defined relative to constraints on what fine-tuning is permitted.
quote: Can you train a model to have property X in such a way that finetuning is unlikely to easily remove property X? If any kind of finetuning is allowed, I think the answer will be "No". So you'd need to place restrictions of the finetuning.
title: comment on: AMA on Truthful AI: Owen Cotton-Barratt, Owain Evans & co-authors
